# net package

Fast CIDR membership testing for IPv4 and IPv6, using sorted binary ranges rather than per-network comparison.

Build a [Networks](/api/net/latest/net.networks/) from a list of CIDR records and ask it whether an address is in any of them — that is the whole API for most callers, and it is what `@imqueue/http-protect` uses for its allow-list. [NetworkList](/api/net/latest/net.networklist/) is the single-family layer underneath, and the [cidrToRange()](/api/net/latest/net.cidrtorange/) and [ipToInt()](/api/net/latest/net.iptoint/) helpers are exported for building something else on the same primitives.

## Remarks

Each network is stored as a start/end address pair in a `Buffer`<!-- -->, sorted, and matched by binary search, so lookup is logarithmic in the number of networks instead of linear. Addresses are compared as `bigint`<!-- -->, which is what makes one code path cover both a 4-byte and a 16-byte address.

The two families never share a buffer, because an IPv6 record is 32 bytes against IPv4's 8 — [Networks](/api/net/latest/net.networks/) holds one [NetworkList](/api/net/latest/net.networklist/) per [NetworkType](/api/net/latest/net.networktype/) and dispatches on the address it is given.

Every CIDR record needs an explicit prefix length. A bare address is rejected, so a single host is `203.0.113.7/32` or `2001:db8::1/128`<!-- -->; passing `203.0.113.7` throws while parsing. Anything that is not a valid record throws rather than being skipped, so one bad entry fails the whole list — validate with [isValid()](/api/net/latest/net.isvalid/) first if the input is untrusted.

## Example 1


```typescript
import { Networks } from '@imqueue/net';

const allowed = new Networks(['10.0.0.0/8', '192.168.0.0/16', '2001:db8::/32']);

allowed.includes('10.1.2.3');     // true
allowed.includes('8.8.8.8');      // false
allowed.includes('2001:db8::1');  // true
```

## Example 2


```typescript
import { isValid, Networks } from '@imqueue/net';

// Untrusted input: check before constructing, because a bad record throws.
const records = input.filter(r => isValid(r.split('/')[0]));
const networks = new Networks(records);
```
